summary: The I2RS architecture in RFC 7921 requires that state written through the interface is ephemeral, meaning it does not persist across a restart. This document describes in detail the requirements for that ephemeral state for any protocol meant to meet I2RS needs.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like writing on a whiteboard rather than carving in stone. The settings are temporary and disappear when things are restarted.

questions: what is ephemeral state in i2rs
how does i2rs handle client conflicts
subtitle: Requirements for temporary routing system configuration that vanishes on restart

tldr.problem: Routing devices need a way for external systems to inject temporary configuration that does not persist across reboots or software restarts, preventing accidental permanent changes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8242 defines detailed requirements for I2RS (Interface to the Routing System) ephemeral state: temporary data stored in a separate datastore that MUST be cleared on reboot, with support from YANG data models, NETCONF and RESTCONF protocols, and conflict resolution when multiple clients try to modify the same data.
tldr.outcome: This provides a standard framework for applications and control systems to temporarily adjust routing behavior without affecting the permanent configuration.

today: RFC 8242 is an Informational RFC describing the requirements that I2RS protocol implementations must satisfy. It has not been obsoleted and remains the standard specification of ephemeral state requirements for I2RS.

sections.title: What Is I2RS and Ephemeral State
sections.content:
RFC 7921 defined the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS), a way for external applications and management systems to inject information into and retrieve information from a router's routing engine. The I2RS architecture introduced the concept of ephemeral state: configuration and operational data that does not survive a reboot of the routing device or the I2RS software running on it.

This document builds on that abstract requirement and spells out exactly what ephemeral state must do. Think of ephemeral state as writing instructions on a whiteboard rather than carving them in stone. When the router restarts, the whiteboard is erased and the original permanent configuration returns.
sections.plainLanguage: Ephemeral state is like a temporary sticky note on a router. When you turn the router off and back on, the sticky note is gone.

sections.title: Core Requirements for Ephemeral State
sections.content:
RFC 8242 establishes 15 key requirements for any I2RS protocol implementation. The first and most important is persistence: ephemeral state MUST NOT survive a reboot, whether hardware or software. If the state must be restored, it should come only from replay actions sent by the I2RS client—the router cannot restore it from a saved backup.

The requirements also cover constraints. Permanent (non-ephemeral) configuration MUST NOT depend on ephemeral state—this would be a validation error. However, ephemeral state can depend on both operational state (like current link status) and non-ephemeral state. The document also mandates support for tracing which I2RS client created or modified each piece of data, using client identity and priority for conflict resolution.
sections.plainLanguage: Ephemeral configuration is like a temporary traffic pattern. Permanent settings cannot depend on it, but it can depend on how things are running right now.

sections.title: Multi-Client Control and Priority
sections.content:
In a shared router, multiple I2RS clients may try to modify the same data at the same time. To handle this, each I2RS client identity has a fixed priority. When two clients attempt to write the same data node and a collision occurs, the protocol uses the priority mechanism to determine which change wins. The highest-priority client's write is accepted; the lower-priority client receives an error notification so it can react to the conflict.

The requirement states that collision resolution must be deterministic. The I2RS architecture recommends a "first write wins" approach, where the first client to succeed owns the data until it releases it. Other deterministic methods that prevent oscillation (clients fighting over the same data back and forth) are also acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: If two remote controllers try to change the same setting at once, the one with higher authority wins, and the loser gets told so it can deal with it.

sections.title: Protocol Support: YANG, NETCONF, and RESTCONF
sections.content:
To implement ephemeral state, I2RS uses existing standard protocols. YANG is the data modeling language; it must support defining modules and schema nodes that are explicitly marked as ephemeral. YANG MUST also be able to augment existing modules with ephemeral nodes.

NETCONF (the Network Configuration Protocol) and RESTCONF (the lighter REST variant) are the protocols that carry I2RS commands. Both must support communication mechanisms so clients can discover whether a router supports I2RS features. Both must also support notifying clients of write conflicts using the priority system described above.

Ephemeral state may exist as both configuration and operational data. The datastore organization must be clear about what is ephemeral and what is permanent.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG describes what ephemeral settings look like. NETCONF and RESTCONF are the protocols that carry commands to change them. Both must tell you when someone else beat you to a change.

sections.title: Multi-Message Operations and Pub/Sub
sections.content:
The requirements do not mandate multi-message atomicity or roll-back. An I2RS protocol may allow multiple operations in one message, but an error in one operation MUST NOT stop additional operations in that message from running, nor can it cause rollback. Multiple messages are allowed too, as long as errors in later messages do not corrupt the ephemeral state.

I2RS clients need to monitor changes to ephemeral state. The requirements call for a publication/subscription mechanism that lets clients subscribe to ephemeral state changes across configuration and operational datastores, with optional filtering to see only ephemeral updates or both ephemeral and operational updates together. Subscriptions themselves can also be ephemeral—when a client disconnects, its subscriptions vanish.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send multiple commands in one go, and if one fails, the others still run. You can also ask to be notified whenever ephemeral settings change.
